title: Specimen Case 1 · Delroy, Grant, Marlon & Alvita (CGT)
scenario:
This exam section is worth 30 marks in total.
1  |  Calculations and workings need only be made to the nearest £.
2  |  All apportionments should be made to the nearest month.
Delroy and Grant
On 10 January 2026, Delroy made a gift of 25,000 £1 ordinary shares in Dub Ltd, an unquoted
trading company, to his son, Grant. The market value of the shares on that date was £240,000.
Delroy had subscribed for the 25,000 shares in Dub Ltd at par on 1 July 2015. Delroy and Grant have
elected to hold over the gain as a gift of a business asset.
Grant sold the 25,000 shares in Dub Ltd on 18 March 2026 for £240,000.
Dub Ltd has a share capital of 100,000 £1 ordinary shares. Delroy was the sales director of the
company from its incorporation on 1 July 2015 until 10 January 2026. Grant has never been an
employee or a director of Dub Ltd.
For the tax year 2025/26, Delroy and Grant are both higher rate taxpayers. They have each made
other disposals of assets during the tax year 2025/26, and therefore they have both already utilised
their annual exempt amount for this year.
Marlon and Alvita
On 28 March 2026, Marlon sold a house for £497,000, which he had owned individually. The house
had been purchased on 22 October 2010 for £152,600.
Throughout the period of ownership, the house was occupied by Marlon and his wife, Alvita, as
their main residence. One-third of the house was always used exclusively for business purposes by
the couple. Business asset disposal relief is not available in respect of this disposal.
For the tax year 2025/26, Marlon is a higher rate taxpayer, but Alvita did not have any taxable
income. This will remain the case for the tax year 2026/27. Neither of them has made any other
disposals of assets during the year.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (Q16–Q20, 2 marks each = 10 marks).

title: Specimen Case 2 · Opal (Inheritance Tax)
scenario:
You should assume that today’s date is 15 March 2026.
Opal is aged 71, and has a chargeable estate for inheritance tax (IHT) purposes valued at £1,025,000.
She owns a property, which is her main residence. It is valued at £374,000 and has an outstanding
repayment mortgage of £160,000. She also holds life insurance on her own life, currently valued at
£350,000, but which will pay proceeds of £442,000 in the event of her death.
Opal owes £22,400 in respect of a personal loan from a bank, and she has also verbally promised
to pay legal fees of £4,600 incurred by her nephew. Opal expects the cost of her funeral to be
£5,200, and this cost will be covered by the £6,000 which she has invested in an individual savings
account (ISA).
Under the terms of her will, Opal has left all of her estate to her children. Opal’s husband is still
alive.
On 14 August 2015, Opal had made a gift of £100,000 to her daughter, and on 7 November 2025,
she made a gift of £220,000 to her son. Both these figures are after deducting all available
exemptions.
You should assume that both the value of Opal’s estate and the nil rate band will remain unchanged
for future years.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (Q21–Q25, 2 marks each = 10 marks).

options.prompt: What is the total net value for the property and insurance policy, which will have been included in the calculation of Opal’s chargeable estate?

–––––––

Tutorial note
Repayment and interest only mortgages should be deducted from the value of the property
in the death estate.
An insurance policy on the life of the deceased should be included in the death estate at the
proceeds received not the market value while they are alive.

title: Specimen Case 3 · Glacier Ltd (VAT)
scenario:
The following information is available in respect of Glacier Ltd’s value added tax (VAT) for the
quarter ended 31 March 2026:
1  |  Invoices were issued for sales of £44,600 to VAT registered customers. Of this figure, £35,200
was in respect of exempt sales and the balance in respect of standard-rated sales. The
standard-rated sales figure is exclusive of VAT.
2  |  In addition to the above, on 1 March 2026 Glacier Ltd issued a VAT invoice for £8,000 plus
VAT of £1,600 to a VAT registered customer in respect of a contract for services which will be
completed on 15 April 2026. The customer paid for the contract in two instalments of £4,800
on 31 March 2026 and 30 April 2026.
3  |  The managing director of Glacier Ltd is provided with free fuel for private mileage driven in
her company car. During the quarter ended 31 March 2026, the total cost of fuel for business
and private mileage was £720, of which £270 was for private mileage. The relevant quarterly
scale rate is £479. All of these figures are inclusive of VAT.
For the quarters ended 30 September 2024, 30 June 2025 and 31 December 2025, Glacier Ltd was
one month late in submitting its VAT returns and in paying the related VAT liabilities. All of the
company’s other VAT returns have been submitted on time.
requirement: Answer all 5 linked Objective Test questions (Q26–Q30, 2 marks each = 10 marks).

options.prompt: What is the amount of output VAT payable by Glacier Ltd in respect of its sales for the quarter ended 31 March 2026?
options.worked_solution:
£3,480
(£9,400 (£44,600 – £35,200) × 20%) + £1,600 = £3,480
Tutorial note
The basic tax point for a supply of services is the date when they are completed, but if a VAT
invoice is issued or payment received before the basic tax point, then this becomes the actual
tax point. Therefore, the tax point for the additional contract is when the VAT invoice was
issued on 1 March.

options.prompt:
Calculate the amounts required to complete the following sentence:
Glacier Ltd will include output VAT of £  |  and input VAT of
£  |  on its VAT return for the quarter ended 31 March 2026 in
respect of the managing director’s company car.
Select the amounts Glacier Ltd will include on its VAT return for the quarter ended 31 March 2026 for output VAT and input VAT on the company car fuel.
options.worked_solution:
Output VAT of £80 and Input VAT of £120
Output VAT £479 × 20/120 = £80
Input VAT £720 × 20/120 = £120

options.prompt: What penalty will Glacier Ltd be charged if the company is 20 days late in submitting its VAT return and paying its VAT liability for the quarter ended 31 March 2026?

options.text: 3% of the VAT liability and £200
3% of the VAT liability
6% of the VAT liability and £200
6% of the VAT liability

options.worked_solution:
A
3% of the VAT liability is charged for paying between 16 and 30 days late.
A £200 penalty is payable for submitting the return late as the threshold of four points has
been reached.
Tutorial note
Glacier Ltd was late in submitting VAT returns for three previous quarters and therefore
already has three penalty points. None of these points are more than two years old and
therefore none have expired. When submitting the return for the quarter ended 31 March
2026 late, Glacier Ltd reaches the threshold of four penalty points and will be charged a £200
penalty.

options.prompt: What is the minimum requirement which Glacier Ltd needs to meet in order to avoid any future penalties?

options.text: Submit four consecutive quarterly VAT returns on time
Submit eight consecutive quarterly VAT returns on time and also pay the related VAT liabilities on time
Submit eight consecutive quarterly VAT returns on time
Submit four consecutive quarterly VAT returns on time and also pay the related VAT liabilities on time

is made to

Glacier Ltd must issue a VAT invoice when it makes a standard-rated supply to a VAT
registered customer. However, there is no requirement to do so if the supply is exempt or if
the supply is to a non-VAT registered customer.
A VAT invoice should be issued within 30 days of the date when the supply is treated as being
made.
